name: Solferino
lede: Solferino is a bluish crimson-red named after an 1859 battle in northern Italy, first used for the new coal-tar fuchsine dye that was also called magenta.

sections.title: A battle turned into a dye
sections.body:
Solferino was the name of a bright bluish-red or crimson dye, taken from the 1859 battle of Solferino in Italy [1][2]. Books disagree on who made the dye. Greenfield credits French chemists with fuchsine in 1859, which some christened solferino or magenta [3]. Finlay says English chemists invented both colors that year [4]. Garfield places production in Lyon and says Britain used solferino first and magenta later [5]. All agree on the names: they commemorate Austrian defeats in Italy in 1859 [3][4][5].

In the Pigment Compendium, solferino is a red-mauve lake based on magenta, and the entry sends the reader there [6]. The same dye family was behind [[mauve]], the first aniline dye, which is why the three colors turn up together in books about the 1850s and 1860s, alongside [[crimson]] [3][5].

sections.title: A fashionable red
sections.body:
Fuchsine was made in far greater quantities than mauve, and was used first for military uniforms and then for the latest fashion [5]. Greenfield adds that Empress Eugénie wore it, as she had worn mauve, in a solferino cashmere petticoat and a matching "Garibaldi" blouse [3]. Finlay notes that the painter J. M. W. Turner just missed these colors, dying before they appeared [4].

The screen swatch here is the Maerz and Paul color of 1930, which they record as first used in 1865 [7]. That is a muted rose-red, nearest in our data to [[mulberry]], not the vivid dye of 1859 [7]. Treat it as the name's dictionary color, not a dye sample.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Solferino is rare in paintings. It appears in 16 of 23,781 paintings in our archive, rarer than 72 per cent of named colors [8]. The earliest dated match is a Chinese painting of 1700, 159 years before the dye existed, and the others are from 1900 and 1903 [8]. That tells us it is a look-alike hue, not the dye. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is a look-alike hue, not a pigment test. [8]

origin.first_recorded: 1859 as a dye; Maerz and Paul date the swatch 1865

disambiguation.gloss: the same dye family; magenta is the name that survived in English

questions.q: True or false: books agree on which country's chemists first made fuchsine in 1859.

openers: Solferino and magenta are the same new red, both named for Italian battles of 1859.
The color of a battle: books disagree on who made the dye, but agree on the name.

issues: Removed claim that Garibaldi led French and Italian forces (sources differ; not all say so)
